title: Book 4 — Melpomene, Chapter 76
paragraphs: This nation too is very averse to adopting foreign customs, rejecting even those of other tribes among themselves, but especially those of the Hellenes—as the histories of Anacharsis and later of Skyles proved. As for Anacharsis, when he was returning to the abodes of the Scythians after having visited many lands and displayed in them much wisdom, he sailed through the Hellespont and put in to Kyzicos. Finding the people of Kyzicos celebrating a festival with great magnificence in honour of the Mother of the gods, Anacharsis vowed to the Mother that if he returned safe and sound to his own land, he would sacrifice to her with the same rites as he saw the men of Kyzicos perform, and also hold a night festival. So when he came to Scythia, he went down into the region called Hylaia (which runs along the racecourse of Achilles and happens to be quite full of all sorts of trees). Into this, I say, Anacharsis went down and proceeded to perform all the ceremonies of the festival in honour of the goddess, with a kettle-drum and with images hung about his person. One of the Scythians perceived him doing this and declared it to King Saulios; the king came himself, and when he saw Anacharsis doing this, shot him with an arrow and killed him. So at the present time, if one asks about Anacharsis, the Scythians say they do not know him—for this reason, that he had gone out of his own country to Hellas and adopted foreign customs. As I heard from Tymnes the steward of Ariapeithes, he was the paternal uncle of Idanthyrsos king of the Scythians, and the son of Gnuros son of Lycos son of Spargapeithes. If then Anacharsis was of this house, let him know he died by the hand of his brother, for Idanthyrsos was the son of Saulios, and it was Saulios who killed Anacharsis.
